title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate the training data or retrieval inputs of AI chatbots by flooding publicly accessible space with synthetic authoritative-looking content. The operation produced a high volume of text formatted to resemble academic research, with citations to legitimate sources, in order to make AI systems more likely to surface pro-Israel framings when users asked about contested policy questions. The failure mode is not one internal to any AI model but one that exploits a structural vulnerability in how large language models and retrieval-augmented systems ingest and weight text that appears credible by surface features.

The point of intervention was upstream of the AI systems themselves, in the environment those systems draw on rather than in their architecture. Catching it would have required either source-vetting processes that flag newly registered domains producing implausibly large volumes of content in a short window, or provenance checks that could detect coordination between multiple nominally independent publications. Neither is a standard part of current AI content pipelines.

What is not established is whether the campaign measurably changed any AI system's outputs, and the reporting notes that Israeli officials themselves expressed doubt about its effectiveness.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The reports presented pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including genocide allegations, war crimes, and Palestinian starvation, all formatted like academic research with citations to legitimate sources. The New York media company Piro Inc registered the site with the U.S. Justice Department as Israeli government material, revealing an effort costing tens of millions of dollars to manipulate how AI systems frame Israeli policy arguments.

The broader campaign involved multiple contractors paid through European advertising group Havas Media, with Clock Tower X receiving $15 million and other firms receiving millions more. Israeli officials have expressed doubt about the campaign's effectiveness, with some calling it a waste of money as American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel. Research shows 60 percent of Americans now view Israel unfavorably, up from 40 percent in 2022, and 31 percent believe Israeli military actions constitute genocide, suggesting that technical manipulation of AI systems cannot overcome public concern about actual policies.
